title: A Harvest for the Choir
premise: Three years after burying her twin sister Zephyra in a coffin that arrived with the wrong name on the death certificate, Xanthe Reyes returns to the drowning town of Marrow Creek to sell the family house. On the porch sits Wren, the imaginary friend they both invented as children, unchanged by time and insisting that in 1974 the town's founding choir took a child who was never returned — and that Zephyra's death was the debt being collected. As Xanthe digs through her grandmother's hymnals and the church's sealed records, she discovers she and Zephyra were swapped at birth, that the 'wrong sibling' in the ground is actually her, and that Wren is the taken child of 1974, kept singing in the choir's keeping. To end the harvest, Xanthe must give the choir a true name and a willing voice — hers — trading her remembered life for Zephyra's, until love against duty forces a third choice: she sings the counter-hymn her grandmother hid inside the official one, unbinding the choir and freeing Wren to finally age, grieve, and die human, while Xanthe walks out of Marrow Creek with half her memories and all of her sister's name.
about_author: Noor Winterbourne is the pseudonym of a former church organist from coastal Oregon who spent a decade transcribing hymnals for small-town historical societies. Their fiction blends folk-horror ritual with quiet, domestic grief, and they claim to have never attended a choir practice that didn't feel like a negotiation.

chapters.title: The Wrong Name on the Stone
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Returning to Marrow Creek for the estate sale, Xanthe visits Zephyra's grave and finds the headstone freshly scrubbed, the dates corrected to Xanthe's own birthdate. She tells herself it's vandalism. Emotional beat: dread dressed up as bureaucratic error, the first crack in her careful rationality.

chapters.title: He Waits on the Porch
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. At the house, Wren sits on the porch swing exactly as he did at age seven — same overalls, same missing tooth. He says, 'You took longer than she did.' Xanthe flees to her car, but the road out loops back to the house. Emotional beat: childhood comfort curdling into captivity.

chapters.title: Hymnal, Annotated
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, with Wren hovering. In the locked piano bench she finds her grandmother's hymnal, its margins dense with corrections to the choir's founding hymn, 'The Harvest Versicle,' dated 1974. Wren flinches from the pages. Emotional beat: the past asserting it left instructions.

chapters.title: What the Town Remembers Differently
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. At the diner, longtime resident Odessa Pell describes the 1974 choir as 'a kindness,' then cannot say a kindness to whom. Every adult gives the same rehearsed sentence. Emotional beat: isolation — the horror of a town that has agreed on its amnesia.

chapters.title: Zephyra's Room, Still Warm
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Zephyra's childhood bedroom smells of her sister's perfume; the bed is made as if slept in last night. Xanthe finds twin diaries with swapped handwriting — Zephyra's diary in Xanthe's script. Emotional beat: grief destabilizing into identity vertigo.

chapters.title: The Choir That Doesn't Disband
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. She attends Sunday service; the choir is eleven voices, and when they sing the Versicle the congregation's faces go smooth and absent, and Xanthe hears a twelfth voice underneath — Wren's, coming from her own mouth. Emotional beat: violation; her body is not fully hers.

chapters.title: Wren Tells It Slant
chapters.summary: Wren's POV, first time. He remembers 1974 as warm: being carried into the church basement by singing neighbors, his mother's hands letting go. He believes he was 'chosen to stay.' He cannot remember his own surname. Emotional beat: tragic innocence — the victim who loves his captors.

chapters.title: Records Sealed in Basement Water
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. In the flooded church basement she retrieves a 1974 birth registry: two Reyes infants born that night, one delivered dead, one alive — and a choir ledger listing 'one voice, in trade' with her grandmother's signature as witness. Emotional beat: the rational explanation dies here.

chapters.title: The Swap
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, interleaved with diary excerpts. The diaries reveal the truth: the living twin was given to the choir; the grandmother substituted the stillborn twin's identity to hide which child survived. Xanthe is the one in the grave. Zephyra lived her sister's name for thirty years. Emotional beat: devastating inversion of grief — she has been mourning herself.

chapters.title: Odessa Breaks Sentence
chapters.summary: Odessa's POV. The old woman, dying and past fear, tells Xanthe the choir takes one voice per generation to keep the town's dead 'in harmony' — and that her own brother went in 1974. She gives Xanthe a tuning fork the brother left behind. Emotional beat: complicity and courage arriving too late, but arriving.

chapters.title: Three Years of Noises, Explained
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Wren walks her through every 'explanation' she invented since the funeral — pipes, raccoons, the settling house — and shows her the truth of each: Zephyra, not at rest, trying to reach her. Emotional beat: guilt transformed into purpose; the noises were love.

chapters.title: The Debt Comes Due
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. The choir's director, soft-spoken Mr. Latch, visits the house with a casserole and a contract: one willing voice, freely given, and Marrow Creek is released — including Zephyra. He is gentle, patient, and utterly certain. Emotional beat: temptation framed as mercy; duty wearing love's face.

chapters.title: Zephyra at the Window
chapters.summary: Zephyra's POV, brief and fragmented. The dead sister reaches through the house's walls, showing Xanthe flashes of the choir's keeping: endless rehearsal, no sleep, no ending. Her only message, scratched in frost: DON'T SING THEIR SONG. Emotional beat: love from beyond, urgent and breaking.

chapters.title: The Counter-Hymn
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Deciphering the grandmother's margin notes, Xanthe reconstructs the counter-hymn hidden inside the Versicle — a melody designed to unbind, written by the grandmother the night of the swap and never sung. Wren refuses to help; the song would end him too. Emotional beat: the plan that requires betraying the friend she came back for.

chapters.title: What Wren Was Before
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Pressed by Xanthe, Wren's memory cracks open: his name was Wren Achebe Pell, Odessa's nephew, and he remembers his mother not letting go — being taken. The warmth was a story the choir taught him. Emotional beat: the imaginary friend discovering he is a stolen child.

chapters.title: Rehearsal for the Harvest
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Latch summons the town to a midnight rehearsal for the fiftieth-anniversary harvest; the whole population attends, smooth-faced, and Xanthe realizes the entire town is collateral, held in the choir's harmony. Emotional beat: the stakes widen from personal to communal; no one gets to opt out.

chapters.title: The Choice at the Grave
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. At her own headstone, Xanthe weighs Latch's offer — sing, free Zephyra, lose herself — against the counter-hymn, which risks everyone. Zephyra's presence and Wren's silence both argue. She chooses the harder song. Emotional beat: love against duty resolved into a third, costlier path.

chapters.title: The Fiftieth Harvest
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs converging. In the church, the choir begins the Versicle; the congregation sways; the walls breathe. Xanthe stands in the pew, the tuning fork in her fist, waiting for the exact bar where her grandmother's correction begins. Emotional beat: held breath, the whole book funneling into a single measure of music.

chapters.title: Counterpoint
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, climax. She strikes the fork and sings the counter-hymn into the Versicle. The harmony tears; Latch unravels into fifty years of borrowed voices; the choir's keeping collapses. Wren, mid-note, begins to age. Emotional beat: ecstatic, terrible release — the song that costs everything it saves.

chapters.title: One Voice, Returned
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Freed, Wren lives his stolen fifty years in a single week — aging, weeping, remembering his mother — and dies at dawn in Odessa's arms, finally a boy with a surname. Emotional beat: grief as grace; the imaginary friend's true funeral, attended by a whole town waking up.

chapters.title: Two Names, One Stone
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV. Zephyra passes over whole; Xanthe, half her memories traded in the singing, buries both names on one stone and sells the house to Odessa's family. She remembers her sister's face but not her own birthday — and finds she can live with the trade. Emotional beat: quiet, scarred peace; identity rebuilt from what remains.

chapters.title: A Harvest for the Choir
chapters.summary: Xanthe's POV, epilogue. Driving out of Marrow Creek, Xanthe passes the church where a new, small, ordinary choir rehearses — children, off-key, alive. On the seat beside her lies the hymnal, its margins blank now. She hums something she doesn't remember learning, and it's just a tune. Emotional beat: the haunting ends not with silence but with music made safe again.
